lessons.title: Organising the daily stud farm routine
lessons.html:
The supervisor's role

A stud farm runs on routine. Mares, foals, youngstock and stallions each have different needs, and the breeding season adds teasing, covering, scanning and foaling to the normal work. The supervisor turns the stud manager's plans into daily tasks, allocates staff, checks the work and reports problems early.

Building the daily plan

TimeTypical activities
Early morningNight foaling report handed over; check all horses; feed and water; treat sick horses
MorningTurn out; teasing of mares; vet visits for scanning; covering sessions; muck out
MiddayFeed youngstock and stabled horses; check water in camps; handle foals
AfternoonBring in horses; farrier and dental work; second covering session if scheduled; yard maintenance
Evening and nightEvening feed; foaling watch on mares close to term; lock up

Allocating staff

  • Match people to tasks by skill: experienced handlers for stallions and covering; trained staff for foaling watch.
  • Draw up a duty roster that covers weekends and night duties fairly, within the hours allowed by the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997.
  • Brief staff each morning: priorities, special cases, vet visit times.
  • Pair new workers with experienced staff.

Checking the work

Walk the stud at least twice a day. Check that every horse has been seen, water is working in every camp, stables are clean, gates are shut and fences are intact. Check the foaling and treatment sheets have been completed and signed.

Health and safety

Stud work is high-risk: stallions, mares protecting foals, and young horses. Make sure staff wear boots and hard hats where needed, use correct handling methods, and that the first aid box and emergency numbers are available. Report all incidents. Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993 both the employer and workers must take reasonable steps to work safely.

Biosecurity

Visiting mares may bring infections. Keep isolation procedures, separate equipment and footbaths where used, and restrict visitors to where they are needed.

lessons.title: Consumables, inventory and the feeding programme
lessons.html:
Monitoring consumables

Consumables are items that are used up: feed, hay, bedding, medicines, dewormers, disinfectants, foaling kit items, gloves, lubricant, bandages, fuel. Running out at the wrong moment, for example of colostrum supplement or disinfectant during foaling season, can cost a foal's life.

  • Set a minimum stock level (re-order point) for each item based on how fast it is used and how long delivery takes.
  • Check stock weekly, and daily for fast-moving items in the season.
  • Order before the re-order point is reached, through the stud's purchasing procedure.
  • Check deliveries against the order and the invoice: quantity, quality, expiry dates.
  • Use stock on a first-in, first-out basis; remove expired medicines for proper disposal.

Maintaining the inventory

The inventory is the register of the stud's assets and equipment: tack, rugs, headcollars, foaling kits, wheelbarrows, tools, machinery, horse boxes. It shows what exists, where it is, its condition, and who is responsible.

ItemNumberLocationConditionLast checked
Foaling kit3Foaling unitComplete01/08
Headcollars (foal size)20Tack room B2 need repair01/08

Do a physical stock-take at set intervals, compare with the register, and investigate differences. Keep the tack and feed rooms locked; control keys.

Supervising the feeding programme

The stud manager or nutritionist sets rations for each group: barren mares, pregnant mares in early and late pregnancy, lactating mares, foals, weanlings, yearlings and stallions. The supervisor makes sure the programme is carried out.

  • Keep feed charts current, by weight, and signed when changed.
  • Check that feeds are made up and given correctly; weigh a sample now and then.
  • Check that creep feed for foals is available where the programme includes it.
  • Monitor body condition of each group every two weeks and report horses that are too thin or too fat.
  • Check grazing: grass cover, water, toxic plants, and when camps need resting.
  • Check feed quality on delivery and in storage; reject mouldy hay or feed.
  • Report feed refusals and digestive problems the same day.

lessons.title: Maintaining stud farm records
lessons.html:
Why records matter

Stud records are used for breed society registration, proving parentage, billing clients, planning matings, veterinary care and showing that the stud meets welfare and legal standards. Incomplete or wrong records can make a foal impossible to register and seriously damage the stud's reputation.

Key stud records

RecordContents
Horse registerName, identity, microchip, markings, owner, date of arrival and departure
Breeding (covering) recordsMare, stallion, dates of teasing and covering, scan results, due date
Foaling recordsDate and time of foaling, sex, colour, markings, placenta passed and checked, foal standing and suckling times, problems
Health and treatment recordsVaccinations, deworming, vet visits, treatments with product, dose, batch, withdrawal notes
Farrier and dental recordsDate and work done
Feed and stock recordsPurchases, usage, stock levels
Staff recordsRosters, hours, training, incidents
Movement recordsHorses in and out, transport details, documents

Good record keeping

  • Record on the day, at the time of the event, not from memory later.
  • Write clearly, in pen, or enter it in the stud's computer system.
  • Sign or initial every entry; date and time it.
  • Correct mistakes with a single line and initials; never use correction fluid or tear out pages.
  • File records so they can be found quickly.
  • Back up computer records regularly.
  • Keep client and personal information confidential and secure, as required by the Protection of Personal Information Act.

Using records to supervise

Review records daily and weekly. Look for trends: a mare who has not been scanned in foal after several coverings, rising treatment numbers in one camp, feed usage higher than the ration. Report findings to the stud manager with suggestions.

Key points

  • Plan the daily routine, allocate staff by skill and check the work twice a day.
  • Set re-order points for consumables and check deliveries and expiry dates.
  • Keep the inventory up to date with regular stock-takes.
  • Make sure feeding follows the programme, by weight, and monitor condition.
  • Record on the day, sign every entry, and never alter records dishonestly.
